"""Starting architecture: the main campaign's default policy (conv encoder, width 64, depth 2, ReLU,
no normalisation), rewritten as a candidate file. A 3x3 conv body, a 1x1 conv placement head
(one logit per brick type and anchor cell), and DONE and value heads on mean+max pooled features."""
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

WIDTH = 64
DEPTH = 2


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        layers, c_in = [], spec.in_channels
        for _ in range(DEPTH):
            layers += [nn.Conv2d(c_in, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()]
            c_in = WIDTH
        self.body = nn.Sequential(*layers)
        self.place_head = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, spec.n_types, 1)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, WIDTH), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.body(obs)
        place = self.place_head(f).flatten(1)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)

analyses.1: There are no trials yet. The baseline seeds (0.068 ×3, 0.258) show bimodal, seed-driven outcomes, so differences under about 0.1 between 2-seed means are probably noise. The default recipe gives only 131072/4096 = 32 PPO updates, and the learning rate decays to 0 over those updates. A policy with roughly 400 actions very likely needs more frequent policy improvement. The budget formula rewards fewer epochs with more samples: 2 epochs gives 243k steps and 1 epoch gives 426k. Round 1 tests three ways to get more updates, each changing one main thing: (A) smaller batches at the same sample count, (B) 2 epochs with smaller batches, and (C) 1 epoch with a higher learning rate. Together these show whether update count, sample count or reuse of each sample matters most.
analyses.2: All three round-1 recipes scored exactly 0.0684 on both seeds. That is the same value as 3 of the 4 baseline seeds (35 of 512 designs). The agent seems to fall into one fixed, repeatable local optimum, probably building only trivial designs well or getting the DONE timing wrong. Changing batch size, epochs or sample count did not move it. Only one baseline seed (0.258) escaped. So the bottleneck looks like exploration and credit assignment, not how fresh the data is or how many updates run. Two levers in the recipe stand out. First, gamma 0.95 shrinks the +1 exact-build bonus to about 0.36 over 20 placements, and to about 0.12 over 41, so the sparse success signal barely reaches early decisions. Second, ent_coef 0.01 may let the policy collapse into the plateau too early. This round tests a longer horizon, stronger entropy, and a combined recipe that also adds more samples.
analyses.3: Seed results split into two groups. Almost every seed ends at exactly 0.0684 (35 of 512 designs), which looks like a fixed local optimum. Seeds that escape it score much higher: 0.258 for the baseline and 0.334 for ent_coef 0.03. Changing the amount of data or the number of updates, and lengthening the horizon, did not help escape. gamma 0.99 lowered training success. Combining ent_coef 0.02 with those changes also failed. The only lead is the stronger entropy bonus (r2c2), and 1 lucky seed out of 2 is weak evidence. The best bet is to raise the chance of escaping the optimum: push entropy further, and test entropy 0.03 alongside a shorter discount and more frequent updates. Every candidate keeps ent_coef at 0.03 or above, so if the effect is real, these trials should give higher 4-seed means in the final re-runs.
analyses.4: Every seed of the default recipe and of the data-volume changes (r1c1–r1c3, r2c3) ended at exactly 0.068. That points to a collapse into one fixed local optimum, not to too little data. Raising entropy is the only change that has escaped it: 3 of 4 seeds at ent 0.03–0.05 escaped, and ent 0.05 escaped on both seeds. Gamma 0.99 hurt. Gamma 0.9 with ent 0.03 gave the best result (0.47 and 0.37, mean 0.418). Both its seeds clearly beat the baseline's 0.068 plateau, so the shorter horizon looks like a real gain, not seed luck. Train success at the end was still only 0.26, so learning probably stops before it plateaus within 32 updates. For the final round I test three extensions of r3c2: stronger entropy (0.05), shorter credit assignment (gae_lambda 0.8), and a higher learning rate. Each could either beat 0.418 or make it more robust across seeds.
